content:
How it works

Future value is what one amount becomes after it grows at a constant rate for a number of years. There are no deposits and no withdrawals. One amount goes in and one amount comes out.

Projected value = starting value * (1 + rate)^years

rate is the annual growth rate divided by 100. The power is the duration in years. Growth compounds once a year, so the second year grows the first year's result rather than the original amount.

  1. Enter the starting value.
  2. Enter the annual growth rate.
  3. Enter the duration in years.
  4. Read the projected value and the total growth.

Total growth is the projected value minus the starting value. The chart below the result plots the value at the end of each year, so you can see where the curve turns steep.

The starting value and the duration must be greater than zero. The growth rate cannot be negative, and a rate of zero returns the starting value unchanged. The duration may be a fraction of a year.

Amounts follow the currency and the number format you choose in settings. The calculation runs in your browser.

Worked examples

100,000 growing at 12 percent for 5 years

The projected value is 176,234.17 and the total growth is 76,234.17.

The first year adds 12,000.00, taking the value to 112,000.00. Add a sixth year and the value reaches 197,382.27. That year adds far more than the first, although the rate never changes. What changes is the base it works on.

2,000,000 growing at 6 percent for 25 years

The projected value is 8,583,741.44 and the total growth is 6,583,741.44.

A rate of 6 percent sounds small next to 12 percent, but 25 years of it more than quadruples the amount. Duration and rate both sit in the exponent, and neither one dominates on its own.

Frequently asked questions

What is the difference between this and the compound interest calculator?

This page grows one amount and compounds once a year. The Compound Interest Calculator also takes a recurring contribution and a compounding frequency. Set that page to yearly compounding with a contribution of 0 and the two agree exactly: 100,000 at 12 percent for 10 years gives 310,584.82 on both.

Can the duration be a fraction of a year?

Yes. 100,000 at 12 percent for 7.5 years gives 233,956.53. The chart draws a point at the end of each whole year and then one last point at 7.5.

Does doubling the growth rate double the result?

No, it does more than that. 100,000 at 12 percent for 5 years reaches 176,234.17, with 76,234.17 of growth. At 24 percent the same amount reaches 293,162.51, with 193,162.51 of growth. The rate sits inside a power, so doubling it multiplies the growth by well over two.

Can I enter a negative growth rate?

No. The lowest rate the page accepts is zero, which returns the starting value unchanged. To measure a fall, put the two amounts into the CAGR Calculator instead. It reports 250,000 falling to 180,000 over 3 years as −10.37 percent a year.

Does the result allow for inflation, fees or taxes?

No. The page applies the one rate you enter, for the number of years you enter, and nothing else. Any cost that reduces the growth has to be inside the rate before you type it.

Is anything I type stored?

No. There is no account and nothing you type is sent to a server. The last 10 results stay while the browser tab is open and go when it closes. The page works with no internet connection.

Good to know

Long durations produce numbers that look implausible until you check them. 1,000,000 at 8 percent for 30 years reaches 10,062,656.89. Nothing unusual happens along the way. The curve is the same shape as the five-year one, seen further along.

This page and the CAGR Calculator are the same equation solved for different unknowns. This one has the rate and wants the ending value. That one has both values and wants the rate. For growth fed by a monthly contribution, use the SIP Calculator.
